hookLine: On the drawing, it looks like the same thing.

lines: IT LOOKS LIKE THE SAME THING.
IT WAS ASKED TO CARRY TWICE AS MUCH.

ACT_1.secondary: In service approximately one year. The atrium is about 117 ft by 145 ft in plan and 50 ft high.

ACT_1.label: Suspended walkways spanning the atrium — at the second, third and fourth floor levels

ACT_1.secondary: The second floor walkway hung from the fourth floor walkway directly above it. The third was offset, on its own rods from the roof framing.
Two 8-inch steel channels laid toe to toe and joined by continuous longitudinal fillet welds. Not a solid section.

ACT_1.quote: As originally designed the fourth and second floor walkways were to be supported by what is referred to as a 'one rod' design.
ACT_1.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988) — the court's description of the original detail

ACT_1.label: Hanger rods — three down each side of the atrium, about thirty feet of threaded steel apiece

ACT_1.quote: The project design criteria specify a design live load of 100 psf (4.8 kPa) for hotel corridors and lobby areas. This is interpreted by NBS to include the walkways
ACT_1.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_1.label: Design load at EACH connection under the one-rod arrangement — NBS Conclusion 6(a)

ACT_1.quote: The AISC Specification for the Design, Fabrication and Erection of Structural Steel for Buildings forms the basis for the steel design provisions of the Kansas City Building Code.
ACT_1.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

items.label: Ultimate capacity the code expected of the one-rod connection — 1.67 × 20.3
Mean ultimate capacity the one-rod connection actually had

ACT_1.label: Of the capacity expected under the AISC Specification — the ORIGINAL detail, before any change (NBS)

ACT_1.quote: The hanger rods and the box beam-hanger rod connections shown on the structural drawings did not meet the design specifications of the Kansas City Building Code.
ACT_1.attribution: Administrative Hearing Commission, quoted at 744 S.W.2d 524 — not contested on appeal

ACT_1.quote: Efforts to obtain copies of the structural design calculations were unsuccessful
ACT_1.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_1.secondary: The Commission found the box beam–hanger rod connections to be special connections. All connections are the responsibility of the structural engineer.

ACT_1.quote: A 'non-redundant' connection which fails will cause collapse of the structure. The box beam-hanger rod connections were 'non-redundant.'
ACT_1.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_1.secondary: A rod. A hole through the box beam. A washer. A nut. Each beam sat on its own nut and put only its own share into the steel.

ACT_2.secondary: The building went up while the drawings were still being drawn.

ACT_2.quote: The steel fabricator on the Hyatt project, Havens Steel Company, had engineers capable of designing simple, complex, or special connections.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: Because of certain fabricating problems Havens proposed to Duncan the use of a 'double rod' system to suspend the second and fourth floor walkways.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: Under this arrangement all of the second floor walkway load was first transferred to the fourth floor box beams, where both that load and the fourth floor walkway load were transmitted through the box beam-hanger rod connections to the ceiling hanger rods.
ACT_2.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

items.label: Second floor connection — unchanged by the redraw

ACT_2.quote: The change in hanger rod arrangement from a continuous rod to interrupted rods essentially doubled the load to be transferred by the fourth floor box beam-hanger rod connections
ACT_2.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982 — Conclusion 6

ACT_2.quote: The effect of this change was to double the load on the fourth floor walkway and the box beam-hanger rod connections on that walkway.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: There was evidence that one of the architects contacted Duncan to verify that the double rod arrangement was structurally sound and was advised by Duncan that it was.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: He called to Duncan's attention questions concerning the strength of the rods and the change from one rod to two. Duncan stated to the technician that the change to two rods was 'basically the same as the one rod concept.'
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.label: Separate occasions on which the project engineer was asked about the implications of the change — the licensing board's investigation, reported in ASCE's journal

ACT_2.quote: Certain information concerning loads and other aspects of the box beam-hanger rod connections which appeared on Duncan's preliminary sketches was not included on the final structural drawings sent to the fabricator.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: The Commission found that the structural drawings (S405.1 Secs. 10 and 11) did not communicate to the fabricator that it was to design the box beam-hanger rod connection, and did communicate to the fabricator that those connections had been designed by the engineer.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: Duncan testified that he intended for the fabricator to design the connections. Havens prepared its shop drawings on the basis that the connections shown on the design drawings had been designed by the structural engineer.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: The Commission found, and appellants do not dispute, that its own internal procedures called for a detailed check of all special connections.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_2.quote: Under the contract, and under the statute, review and approval of the shop drawings is an engineering function.
ACT_2.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_3.secondary: With the hotel still going up, the atrium roof collapsed. The investigation established that the cause was poor construction workmanship.

ACT_3.quote: In their report to the architects, appellants advised 'we then checked the suspended bridges and found them to be satisfactory.'
ACT_3.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_3.quote: Appellants did not do a complete check of the design of all steel in the atrium nor a complete check of the suspended bridges.
ACT_3.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_3.quote: With this change in hanger rod arrangement, the ultimate capacity of the walkways was so significantly reduced that, from the day of construction, they had only minimal capacity to resist their own weight and had virtually no capacity to resist additional loads imposed by people.
ACT_3.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_3.secondary: Kansas City is hot. The hotel has been in service about a year.

ACT_3.quote: Between 1,500 and 2,000 area residents chose to escape the heat at the Hyatt Regency Hotel's tea dance, a weekly event featuring big band music and a dance contest.
ACT_3.attribution: Pfatteicher, “‘The Hyatt Horror’”, ASCE Journal of Performance of Constructed Facilities 14(2), May 2000

events.text: Crowd in atrium area is estimated at 1500 to 2000
Band returns from break and begins to play for dance contest
Second and fourth floor walkways collapse

lines: NO BEND. NO SAG. NO WARNING.

ACT_3.quote: Thus, failure of any one connection would have led to complete collapse of the walkway system.
ACT_3.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_3.quote: In the collapse, the second and fourth floor walkways fell to the atrium floor, with the fourth floor walkway coming to rest on top of the lower walkway.
ACT_3.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_3.quote: Most of those killed or injured were either on the first floor level of the atrium or on the second floor walkway. The third floor walkway was not involved in the collapse.
ACT_3.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982 — executive summary

ACT_3.label: Pounds — the weight of the two walkways, the Missouri Court of Appeals' figure
Tons of steel and concrete, from four storeys up — our own arithmetic on the NBS dead-load measurement

events.text: A call goes out for cutting tools
More than a hundred firefighters in the building
The first walkway span is lifted

ACT_3.secondary: 7:05 p.m. to 4:30 a.m. The federal report gives it eleven lines.

ACT_3.label: People died. At least 186 were injured — the Missouri Court of Appeals' figures

ACT_3.secondary: Neither the federal report nor the court names a single victim. This film names none of the dead.

ACT_4.secondary: Three days after. Senator Eagleton's office contacts the National Bureau of Standards; on 22 July the Mayor formally requests it.

ACT_4.quote: In the early phases of the investigation, NBS involvement was limited by court order to visual and photographic observations and measurements.
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_4.secondary: National Bureau of Standards, May 1982. Not NIST — the Bureau did not become the Institute until 1988.

ACT_4.quote: Collapse of the walkways occurred under the action of loads that were substantially less than the design loads specified by the Kansas City Building Code.
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982 — Conclusion 1

ACT_4.quote: it is concluded that the most probable cause of failure was insufficient load capacity of the box beam-hanger rod connections.
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_4.quote: Two factors contributed to the collapse: inadequacy of the original design for the box beam-hanger rod connection, which was identical for all three walkways, and a change in hanger rod arrangement during construction that essentially doubled the load on the box beam-hanger rod connections at the fourth floor walkway.
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

items.label: Design load at the connection AS DRAWN (one rod)
Design load at the fourth floor connection AS BUILT (two rods)

ACT_4.quote: It would be expected that the ultimate load capacity of the resulting connection would be at least 1.67 times 40.7, or 68 kips (302 kN)
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982

ACT_4.quote: Mean ultimate capacities of the fourth floor box beam-hanger rod connections were estimated on the basis of the NBS test series and these capacities ranged from 18.2 kips (81 kN) to 19.3 kips (86 kN) with an average value of 18.6 kips (83 kN)
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982 — Conclusion 2(c)

items.label: Ultimate load the code required of the connection
Ultimate capacity the connection actually had

ACT_4.label: Maximum load on a fourth floor connection at the moment of collapse (NBS)

lines: THE STRENGTH RATIO IS ABOUT 27% — OURS, NOT THEIRS.

ACT_4.label: The load on the night, measured against the 40.7 kip design load (NBS)

ACT_4.quote: Neither the quality of workmanship nor the materials used in the walkway system played a significant role in initiating the collapse
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982 — Conclusion 9

ACT_4.quote: Dynamic loads induced by walking or dancing on the walkways would not have been significant in comparison to the static loads.
ACT_4.attribution: NBS Building Science Series 143, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse, May 1982 — Conclusion 1(c)

ACT_4.label: Credible upper-bound combined occupancy of the second and fourth floor walkways at the time of collapse, as NBS counted it

lines: WITHOUT THE CHANGE IT WAS STILL ILLEGAL.
WITHOUT THE CHANGE IT WOULD HAVE HELD.

ACT_5.label: Paid out by insurers to settle civil suits as at December 1983 — a figure at a date, not a final total

ACT_5.secondary: The Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors files its complaint.

ACT_5.label: Days of hearing before the Missouri Administrative Hearing Commission

ACT_5.quote: Its 'Statement of the case, Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Decision' are 442 pages in length.
ACT_5.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_5.secondary: 98 pages of findings of fact, 322 of conclusions of law, 180 numbered findings. The appellants challenged five.
Gross negligence in the preparation and completion of a structural drawing; misconduct in misrepresenting to the architects the safety of a connection.
Vicariously liable for the acts and omissions of the project engineer; grossly negligent in failing to review, or assure review of, the drawing before affixing his seal.

ACT_5.quote: By section 327.411.2 the owner of the seal is responsible for the 'whole ... engineering project' when he places his seal on 'any plans' unless he expressly disclaims responsibility and specifies the documents which he disclaims.
ACT_5.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_5.quote: The responsibility for the structural integrity and safety of the walkway connections was Duncan's and that responsibility was non-delegable.
ACT_5.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_5.quote: while the engineer may properly delegate the work of performing engineering design functions, he cannot delegate the responsibility
ACT_5.attribution: the administrative law judge, quoted in Pfatteicher, “‘The Hyatt Horror’”, ASCE Journal of Performance of Constructed Facilities 14(2), May 2000

ACT_5.quote: The Commission defined the phrase in the licensing context as 'an act or course of conduct which demonstrates a conscious indifference to a professional duty.'
ACT_5.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988) — gross negligence, defined for the first time in a Missouri licensing case

ACT_5.quote: The structural engineer's duty is to determine that the structural plans which he designs or approves will provide structural safety because if they do not a strong probability of harm exists. Indifference to the duty is indifference to the harm.
ACT_5.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_5.quote: That breach occurred at the latest when their design was incorporated into the building with their approval and they were subject to discipline whether or not any collapse subsequently occurred.
ACT_5.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988)

ACT_5.quote: the original inadequacies of the structural drawings might not have been critical if a meaningful review of the shop drawings had occurred.
ACT_5.attribution: Duncan v. Missouri Board for Architects, Professional Engineers and Land Surveyors, 744 S.W.2d 524 (Mo. Ct. App. 1988) — footnote 7

events.text: The Board revokes all three certificates
ASCE conduct committee: expel, with no privilege ever to rejoin
One finding reversed; the revocations stand

ACT_5.quote: Engineers shall hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public in the performance of their professional duties
ACT_5.attribution: ASCE Code of Ethics, Fundamental Canon 1, as rewritten in 1976

ACT_5.secondary: The conduct committee recommended expulsion. The board of direction voted to suspend for three years; he then relinquished his membership. The project engineer faced no ethics committee at all.

items.label: 18.6 kips — as the steel could actually give

lines: ONE BEAM WAS ASKED TO CARRY TWO.

ENDING.quote: In their place stands a single span, supported not by delicate, graceful rods, but standing on stout, sturdy columns
ENDING.attribution: Pfatteicher, “‘The Hyatt Horror’”, ASCE Journal of Performance of Constructed Facilities 14(2), May 2000 — as at 2000

ENDING.secondary: A court of appeals, January 1988. Nothing here is said about what either engineer has done since.

ENDING.label: People went to a tea dance and did not come home

ENDING.secondary: A rod, a washer, a nut, and a hole through a welded steel beam.

_readme: Provenance for figures_by_section. One entry per beat, in the same order, so a reader can check any card against EP69_hyatt_FACTS_LEDGER.v001.md (138 rows, 140 verbatim quotations, verifier green 140/140). ledger_rows are the row ids behind every factual assertion on that card; card_window is where build_case_film_generic.build_figures() will place it against the MEASURED master; lands_on is the narration it sits over, taken from 06_audio/narration_index.v001.json. Nothing here is read by any tool.

PLACEMENT. build_figures() does not read a per-beat time: it spaces a section's payloads EVENLY inside the section window (dur 6.0s, and 3.0s in HOOK/OP), reserving 3.0s at the head and 6.5s at the tail. ORDER and COUNT are therefore the only placement controls. Both were chosen against the delivered narration index, not against the paper design, and card_window/lands_on above were computed with the same arithmetic build_figures uses. Every beat was checked to overlap narration it actually illustrates.

BEAT COUNTS. episode_spec figure_beats_per_act is [14, 18]. ACT_1..ACT_5 each carry 18, the ceiling, because this film's argument IS a sequence of measured numbers and every one of them needs to be seen. HOOK 3, OP 1, ENDING 8 -- those three are not acts and the floor does not apply to them.

SACRIFICIAL SLOTS. build_figures overwrites figures[0] and figures[-1] of the whole sorted list with the AI-disclosure lowerthird. HOOK[0] and ENDING[-1] are therefore already that card, so no content beat is destroyed (EP65's v001 lost its closing line this way).

THE DESIGNED SILENCES, and the one card that sits on one. The delivered master carries 30.0 s of scripted silence, measured off this index as three inter-chunk gaps: 22.0 s after VC-0074 (the H2 assembly opening ACT_2), 5.5 s after VC-0173 (H5 pull-through 3.0 + black 2.5, before the 7:05 PM card) and 2.5 s after VC-0209 (the TURN). Every beat above was checked against all three. ONE overlaps: ACT_1[17], 294.6-300.6, six seconds inside the 22.0 s hold. It cannot be moved -- build_figures reserves only 6.5 s at a section tail and this hold is 22 s long, so the last ACT_1 card lands inside it at every count in the declared band (14 -> 292.5, 18 -> 294.6). Rather than hide it, that slot is authored FOR the hold: it names the four parts the wordless animation is assembling and asserts nothing outside DS-04/DS-05/DS-06. The other two holds are clear.

THE SIX NUMBERS. 20.3 -> 40.7 -> 68 -> 18.6 -> 21.4 -> 114. Six AE kinetic beats are separately authored at scripts/ae/jobs_ep69_hyatt.json and are CUTS, not figures. The figure grid deliberately carries the same numbers as compbars/numberticker so the argument survives if the owner drops any AE beat. NOTE: the AE _at timecodes (3:07 / 6:37 / 14:55 / 17:13 / 17:49 / 28:15) were derived from FILM BIBLE 12.5, whose clock is the word-cumulative model at 160.0 wpm and does NOT charge the 30.0s of designed silence. Against the delivered master every beat after the 22.0s ACT_2 hold moves later. Re-time them from this narration index before placing them in hyatt_film.json.

THE LOAD RATIO. Every card that states 31 percent says out loud that it is a LOAD ratio (21.4 against 68), and that the capacity ratio (18.6 against 68, about 27 percent) is OUR arithmetic and is not NBS's. Quarantine -01 and ledger LD-11/LD-12 make this the single most likely factual error in the episode; the Missouri Court of Appeals itself makes the slip in its own footnote 12.

QUOTE CARDS ARE VERBATIM, AND CHECKED. 43 of the 102 beats are `quote` cards. Each was string-matched back into EP69_hyatt_FACTS_LEDGER.v001.md after this file was written: 42 match the ledger byte for byte. The 43rd, ACT_4[3] (NBS Conclusion 1), deliberately does NOT: the cached OCR of BSS 143 carries the fault `specif ied` and the ledger says out loud that on screen and in narration the word is `specified`. Do not 'correct' that card back to the scanner's error.
AGENCY AND DATE. Quarantine -21: it is NBS, it is the National Bureau of Standards, and it is May 1982. ACT_4[2] is the card that fixes it on screen. No card anywhere says NIST.

NO DEPICTION. Quarantines -10, -11, -12 and -13 bar third-party footage, any depiction of a casualty or of the occupied room at or near 7:05 p.m., and any real likeness. Every beat here is typography, a diagram, or a number; none asserts an image of the room, and ACT_3[17] states on screen that the film names none of the dead (ND-09).

ATTRIBUTION. Every `quote` card names the tribunal or the document it comes from, because the film's rule is that criticism is a finding and never the narrator's opinion. 142,000 lb and 114 are attributed to the Missouri Court of Appeals (quarantine -06, -03), never to the federal report.

LEDGER ROWS SPOKEN BUT NOT CARDED (the grid has fewer slots than the script has lines): EV-03 partly, CH-07/CH-09, RV-02/RV-03/RV-04/RV-05, FN-03/FN-04/FN-13/FN-14, LD-02/LD-05/LD-07/LD-16/LD-18/LD-19, DC-17, PR-06/PR-07, ND-01/ND-02. All are narrated; none is contradicted by any card above.

STILL MISSING FOR THIS EPISODE, and unchanged by this file: episodes/PD-2026-069-hyatt/05_visuals/asset_manifest.v001.json, the 113 mandatory stills and >=40 factory clips under remotion/public/hyatt/, the face-plate register, and an Ep69Hyatt composition in remotion/src/Root.tsx. build_case_film_generic --dry-run stops at the asset manifest, before it ever reaches these figures.
